newsitem.title: UK: The Proteus Column - George Town Re.
newsitem.headline: The Proteus Column - George Town Re.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

The Alternative Risk Transfer market is developing, but slowly. One reason is the state of insurance and reinsurance markets where historically low rates mean low cost capacity is available for most lines of business.

Two other reasons are the cost of developing new ways of raising capital and the time needed to design alternative risk transfer mechanisms. A few products have been launched and more are in the pipeline, but insurers, like other commercial enterprises, are generally unwilling to talk about new ideas for the good reason many never make it off the drawing board.

One exception is St Paul Re, which is keen to talk about its George Town Re scheme launched late last year. Effectively St Paul Re acts as an underwriting manager for the 20 or so institutional investors who together have put $68.5 million into George Town Re.

St Paul doesn't own the Cayman Islands based company, but the arrangement allows it to write more business without any impact on its balance sheet. It also means that St Paul Re can get more out of its existing staff and systems, meet customer demand and, theoretically, have more influence over rates.

The investors, who choose between two levels of risk, stand to earn attractive yields as long as claims on the business underwritten don't go above certain levels. St Paul Re says the business is widely spread and the risk therefore low.

The scheme, which was developed in concert with Goldman Sachs, took longer to bring to fruition than St Paul originally expected. The costs of the project were almost certainly higher than planned, both because of the time-scale and that fact that St Paul and Goldman Sachs had to explain it to a lot of institutional investors.
Also the amount raised was lower than the original target of $100 million, but St Paul said it is pleased with the outcome, both in its own right and as a learning experience.

It expects to use its George Town Re experience as a blueprint for similar ventures in the future which will give it a lead over the competition. It also sees the possibility of much bigger capital raising exercises in the future.
Although such schemes are regarded as innovative, there is more than a fleeting resemblance between George Town Re and a well-known insurance market.
For three hundred years Lloyd's of London has provided an opportunity for investors to place their money with insurance professionals who then use it to fund their underwriting business.
The Lloyd's concept has come under much criticism for understandable reasons in recent years and many Lloyd's operators are now moving towards becoming more like conventional companies.

However, the fact that other insurers are now adopting a similar mechanism to do business suggests that perhaps the basic Lloyd's principle is not as flawed as the market's losses and problems since 1988 might suggest.
